Blind means unable to see. A person who is blind cannot perceive light, shapes, or images through their eyes — either partially or completely. The condition can exist from birth or develop later due to illness or injury.

  • She has been blind since birth.
  • The accident left him blind in his left eye.

Notice that "blind in one eye" is perfectly natural — blindness can affect one or both eyes.
The Big Idea Behind All Its Meanings

Before going further, here is the single idea that connects every use of this word:

Blind always describes the absence of sight or perception — whether that perception is physical (using your eyes), mental (understanding something), or emotional (noticing something).

Keep this in mind, and every other meaning will make instant sense.

In everyday speech, blind is used figuratively far more often than literally. It describes situations where something that should be visible or noticeable is simply not seen — not because of a medical condition, but because of emotion, ignorance, choice, or circumstance.

1. Blind to something — failing to notice or acknowledge something

When someone is blind to a fact, a flaw, or a situation, they are unable or unwilling to see it. Their eyes work fine, but their mind does not register what is there.

  • She was completely blind to his dishonesty.
  • He is blind to the effect his words have on others.

This often implies a kind of emotional shield — the person cannot see the truth because they do not want to, or because they are too deeply involved.

2. Blind faith / blind obedience / blind trust — following without questioning

When blind modifies nouns like faith, obedience, loyalty, or trust, it means doing something entirely, without applying your own judgment, without asking for reasons, and without looking at the evidence. You move forward without "seeing" where you are going.

  • Blind obedience to authority is dangerous.
  • She placed blind trust in a company that later cheated her.
  • He followed his leader with blind loyalty.

The tone here is usually cautionary. The suggestion is that the person should have looked more carefully before committing so fully.

3. Blind with emotion — overwhelmed to the point of losing judgment

When an emotion is described as making someone blind, it means the feeling is so intense that the person cannot think straight. Reason, caution, and awareness are temporarily "switched off."

  • Blind with rage, he said things he deeply regretted.
  • She was blind with grief after losing her father.
  • Jealousy can make a person blind to the consequences of their actions.

The emotion here functions like a blindfold — it blocks the ability to perceive clearly.

4. Done without prior knowledge or information

Blind can describe an action or situation where the person involved does not have the information that would normally help them make a good decision. Something important is hidden or unknown.

  • A blind date is a romantic meeting between two people who have never met and know nothing about each other beforehand.
  • A blind tasting (wine, food, etc.) is one where the labels or identities are hidden, so the taster judges purely on experience, not on reputation or expectation.
  • A blind audition is one where the judges cannot see the performer — they evaluate only the sound, not the person's appearance or identity.
  • Flying blind means attempting something without the information, tools, or guidance you would normally rely on.

In all these cases, something that would ordinarily be visible is deliberately or unavoidably hidden.

5. Physical/spatial — a place where your view is blocked

When describing a physical location, blind means that your line of sight is cut off — you cannot see what lies beyond or around it.

  • A blind corner on a road is one where you cannot see oncoming traffic until you have already turned into it.
  • A blind bend is a curve in a road where visibility ahead is severely limited.
  • A blind wall is a wall with no windows, doors, or openings.
  • A blind alley is a narrow street that is sealed at one end — a dead end.

6. Blind alley (figurative) — a path that leads nowhere

Beyond its literal meaning, a blind alley also describes a plan, approach, or line of thinking that ultimately produces no useful result.

  • After months of research, the team realized they had been following a blind alley.
  • That negotiation strategy turned out to be a blind alley.

7. Blind spot — an area of invisible weakness

Literally, a blind spot is a small area in the human eye's field of vision that cannot detect light (due to where the optic nerve connects). On the road, it refers to the area around a vehicle that the driver cannot see in any mirror.

Figuratively — and this is the more common use — a blind spot is a subject, type of person, or area of life where someone consistently fails to see clearly or think objectively. It is a personal weakness they are unaware of.

  • His blind spot is his own ego — he genuinely cannot see when he is being arrogant.
  • Every great thinker has blind spots.
  • That critic has a blind spot when it comes to foreign films.

Blind often combines with other words to form compound adjectives.

Colour-blind (or color-blind) literally means unable to distinguish between certain colours (most commonly red and green). Figuratively, saying someone is "colour-blind" in a social sense means they treat all people equally regardless of race or background — they do not "see" racial difference.

Snow-blind means temporarily unable to see because of the intense glare of sunlight reflecting off snow.

Blind-drunk is an informal expression, mostly used in British English, meaning extremely, severely intoxicated — so drunk that one's perception and awareness are almost completely gone.
"Turn a Blind Eye" — A Key Phrase

This well-known phrase means to deliberately choose to ignore something you know is happening — to pretend you have not noticed.

  • The teacher turned a blind eye to the students passing notes.
  • The government turned a blind eye to the corruption in its own ranks.

The phrase implies a conscious, deliberate choice to look away, often when it would be inconvenient or uncomfortable to acknowledge the truth.

Blind is not always all-or-nothing. Language often uses it in degrees:

  • Someone can be almost blind (very limited vision), legally blind (vision below a certain threshold as defined by law), or completely blind.
  • Someone can be somewhat blind to an issue (partially aware) or utterly blind to it (completely unaware).
  • Blind faith can range from mildly uncritical to dangerously unquestioning.

In modern usage, many people — especially disability advocates — prefer terms like visually impaired or person with low vision when referring to someone's medical condition, as these feel less reductive. However, blind remains the standard, widely accepted adjective in medical, legal, and everyday contexts, and there is nothing inherently wrong with using it respectfully.
Summary: The One Thread Through Everything

No matter which meaning you encounter, blind always points to the same root idea: something that should be perceived — seen, understood, or noticed — is not. Whether it is a person without sight, someone ignoring a problem, a road where you cannot see ahead, or a test where labels are hidden, the word always signals an absence of perception or visibility. That is the heart of blind.
